title: Bias, variance, and MSE
dek: Bias is E[θ̂] − θ. Variance is the scatter of θ̂. MSE adds their squares. Unbiasedness is not a virtue if the variance explodes.
story: Fix a procedure T_n(Y). Bias_θ(T_n) = E_θ[T_n] − θ. That expectation is over the sampling model, at a hypothetical true θ. A single printed estimate does not have a bias; the procedure does.

MSE = Var(T_n) + Bias². The MLE is often asymptotically unbiased and efficient in regular models, and still dominated in MSE by a shrinkage estimator when n is small or p is large. Hierarchical models in this studio are organised shrinkage, not a confession.

Consistency is a limit: T_n →p θ as n → ∞. Finite-sample unbiasedness does not imply consistency if variance refuses to die, and consistency does not imply unbiasedness at the n you have (π̂(1−π̂) for a Bernoulli variance is biased but consistent).
deepTitle: When unbiasedness is the wrong god
deep: Cramér–Rao (regular, unbiased): Var(θ̂) ≥ 1 / I(θ). Attaining the bound is “efficiency” in that narrow class. MLEs do it asymptotically. A biased estimator may beat the bound in MSE — James–Stein, empirical Bayes, penalised likelihood.

Sample variance: s² = (n−1)⁻¹ ∑ (yᵢ − ȳ)² is unbiased for Gaussian σ²; the MLE uses n in the denominator and is biased low. For n = 8 MIC replicates, that distinction is not pedantry. For n = 800 WGS isolates on a well-estimated mean, it is.

Shrinkage toward a hierarchical mean increases bias for each unit and cuts variance enough that MSE falls for the small units. That is the eight-districts geometry later in this wave. Calling it “biased therefore invalid” is a confusion of loss functions.

Misspecification bias is not the same as estimator bias under a true model. Omitted variables bias OLS for a causal coefficient even when OLS is unbiased for the population projection coefficient. Name the target functional before you say “unbiased.”

example.title: Bernoulli variance estimator
example.setup: Yᵢ iid Bernoulli(π), n = 5, π = 0.2. Compare the MLE of the variance v = π(1−π), which is π̂(1−π̂), to the unbiased-for-π plug-in myth.

steps.title: Target
steps.body: v = π(1−π) = 0.16. Estimator v̂ = π̂(1−π̂) with π̂ = ȳ.

steps.title: Bias exists
steps.body: E[π̂] = π so π̂ is unbiased for π, but g(π) = π(1−π) is concave near 0.2, so E[g(π̂)] ≠ g(E[π̂]) by Jensen. v̂ is biased low in small n. Consistency still holds because π̂ →p π.

steps.title: MSE vs a constant
steps.body: A ridiculous estimator v̂ ≡ 0.16 is unbiased at this particular π and has zero variance — and is useless everywhere else. Unbiasedness at one parameter value is not a method.

example.takeaway: State the target functional. Unbiasedness is a property of a pair (procedure, functional), not a halo.

check.prompt: A shrinkage estimator that is biased for each unit-level θⱼ can still be preferable because:
choices: Bias is imaginary in Bayesian procedures
MSE can fall when the variance drop beats Bias², especially for small nⱼ
Unbiasedness is required by Wilks’ theorem
check.answer: MSE can fall when the variance drop beats Bias², especially for small nⱼ
check.why: That is the bias–variance trade. Hierarchical means are built on it.

whyWrong.Bias is imaginary in Bayesian procedures: Bayes estimators have frequentist bias; they may still have good MSE or calibration.
whyWrong.Unbiasedness is required by Wilks’ theor: Wilks is about nested LRTs, not this.
whyWrong.Fisher information forbids biased estima: Cramér–Rao is a bound for unbiased regular estimators.

check.prompt: If Bias = 2 and Var = 5, MSE equals:
check.why: MSE = Var + Bias² = 5 + 4 = 9. Do not add Bias without squaring.

whyWrong.7: That is Var + Bias, missing the square.
whyWrong.25: That is (Bias+Var)² or Var², not the decomposition.

check.prompt: On the MSE small-multiples, why does complete pooling look worse in the large district?
choices: Because a large district’s own data already have small variance, so shrinking toward a shared mean mostly adds bias
Because MSE is undefined for n>30
check.answer: Because a large district’s own data already have small variance, so shrinking toward a shared mean mostly adds bias
check.why: Partial pooling interpolates: small nⱼ shrink, large nⱼ do not. Complete pooling cannot stop shrinking.

whyWrong.Because pooling has no bias: Complete pooling is badly biased for heterogeneous units.
whyWrong.Because no-pooling is always inadmissibl: James–Stein is a specific result; the plate is a cartoon of nⱼ.
